hook.text: All the world's data fits in a mug of DNA — nature's storage holds a million times more data per gram than a hard drive.

buildup.text: Binary data is converted to DNA bases — A, T, G, C replace 0s and 1s, then synthetic DNA is manufactured to store the file.

discovery.text: Microsoft and the University of Washington stored 200 MB in DNA — including a music video, retrieved with zero errors.

twist.text: Writing DNA costs $800 per megabyte — a million times more expensive than magnetic tape. Cost must drop 6 orders of magnitude.

climax.text: DNA lasts thousands of years without power — woolly mammoth genomes survived 10,000 years in permafrost. No server room needed.

punchline.text: Store everything in DNA — nature's hard drive holds data for millennia.

quiz.question: What is the main barrier to widespread DNA data storage adoption?
options: DNA cannot store digital information accurately
Synthesizing DNA for data storage costs roughly a million times more per megabyte than conventional storage
DNA degrades too quickly to be useful for archival storage

details.summary: DNA data storage encodes digital information in synthetic DNA sequences, offering extraordinary density and longevity. A single gram of DNA can theoretically store 215 petabytes of data, and properly preserved DNA remains readable for thousands of years.
details.whyItMatters: Global data production is outpacing storage technology. DNA offers a storage medium that is incredibly dense, durable for millennia, and requires no electricity to maintain. It could solve the long-term archival storage crisis facing humanity.
takeaways: One gram of DNA can store 215 petabytes of digital information theoretically
DNA remains readable for thousands of years when properly preserved
Current costs are falling but remain too high for routine data storage

faq.question: How is digital data encoded into DNA?
faq.answer: Binary data is converted to a quaternary code using DNA's four bases: A, T, G, and C. Error-correcting codes add redundancy. Short synthetic DNA strands are manufactured, each containing a data payload and addressing index. Reading uses DNA sequencing to recover the original data.

faq.question: When will DNA data storage become practical?
faq.answer: Current costs of synthesis and sequencing make DNA storage impractical for everyday use. However, for long-term archival data accessed rarely, economics are improving. Enzymatic DNA synthesis and nanopore sequencing advances could make it viable for cold storage within a decade.
